title: Intestinal Protozoa and Helminths: Stool Examination Essentials
summary: A bench-level guide to stool collection and preservation, direct wet mounts, formalin-ethyl acetate concentration, and permanent staining, followed by the morphology of the key intestinal protozoa (Entamoeba, Giardia, Cryptosporidium and the coccidia) and helminth eggs and larvae (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris, Enterobius, Taenia, Strongyloides), with the classic exam traps that separate species and the artifacts that fake them.
objectives: Select the correct stool preservative for each examination method and explain why formalin-fixed material cannot be permanently stained.
Perform and interpret direct wet mounts, formalin-ethyl acetate concentration, trichrome and iron hematoxylin permanent stains, and modified acid-fast stains for coccidia.
Differentiate Entamoeba histolytica from Entamoeba coli cysts and explain why morphology cannot separate E. histolytica from E. dispar.
Recognize the diagnostic eggs and larvae of the major intestinal helminths and the specimen types required for Enterobius and Strongyloides.
Distinguish true parasite stages from common artifacts and apply the classic exam traps to stool cases.

highYield: Morphology cannot distinguish Entamoeba histolytica from E. dispar; report the E. histolytica/dispar complex unless a specific antigen test or PCR resolves it.

PVA fixative preserves the specimen for permanent stained smears (trichrome, iron hematoxylin); 10 percent formalin preserves eggs, cysts, and larvae for concentration and wet mounts but prevents permanent staining.
Giardia lamblia cysts are oval with 2 to 4 nuclei and curved median bodies; trophozoites are pear-shaped with two nuclei giving an owl-face appearance.

Helminth eggs: Ascaris (mammillated coat), hookworm (thin shell, morula of 4-8 cells), Trichuris (barrel with bipolar mucoid plugs), Enterobius (D-shaped, larvated, diagnosed by cellophane tape), Taenia (radially striated embryophore with 6-hooked oncosphere), Strongyloides (larvae, not eggs, in stool).
Cryptosporidium oocysts (4-6 micrometers) and the other coccidia are detected with modified acid-fast staining or antigen methods; routine trichrome can miss them.
Enterobius vermicularis eggs are deposited around the anus, not in stool; the standard collection is a morning cellophane tape swab before bathing or defecation.

quickReview.mnemonic: For Entamoeba cysts: 'Cultured ladies eat 4-course meals' - E. coli has up to 8 nuclei, E. histolytica/dispar up to 4 (hista-FOUR-ka).

deepStudy.introduction: Stool parasitology is one of the last truly morphology-dependent corners of the clinical laboratory, and it is a heavily tested area in Philippine review programs because a surprising number of infections are still diagnosed by looking down the microscope. The workflow is simple on paper: collect the specimen correctly, examine a fresh wet mount, concentrate the material, and prepare a permanent stained smear - but every step hides a decision that changes what you can report. A specimen dropped into the wrong fixative cannot be stained; a cold wet mount kills trophozoite motility; an over-decolorized modified acid-fast smear hides Cryptosporidium. After the methods come the organisms: amebae whose species names outrun their morphology, flagellates with unforgettable shapes, coccidia small enough to be dismissed as debris, and a lineup of helminth eggs whose coats, plugs, and internal cell counts do the identifying. This lesson builds the bench logic first, then walks through the protozoa and helminths with the comparison tables and traps that exam writers love: Trichuris versus hookworm, E. coli versus E. histolytica cysts, Enterobius that never appears on routine stool, Strongyloides that shows larvae instead of eggs, and the artifacts - pollen, yeast, starch, Charcot-Leyden crystals - that pretend to be parasites.

sections.heading: Stool collection, preservation, and the examination algorithm
sections.body: The examination algorithm starts before the specimen reaches the bench. A fresh, unpreserved specimen is required for the direct wet mount (saline for motility and general morphology; iodine to bring out nuclear detail and glycogen) and for any motility assessment, because trophozoites stop moving and degenerate quickly - examine promptly, ideally within 30 minutes of passage, and keep the specimen warm. For routine ova and parasite workup, laboratories commonly request three specimens collected on alternate days (or three early-morning specimens for some organisms) because shedding is intermittent and a single stool misses infections. Two fixatives carry the rest of the workflow. Ten percent formalin preserves eggs, cysts, and larvae indefinitely and is the fixative used for concentration procedures and unstained wet mounts, but formalin cross-links proteins so a formalin-fixed specimen cannot be made into a permanent stained smear. Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) fixative - including modern mercury-free and zinc-based PVA formulations - is the fixative for permanent stained smears: the specimen is fixed in PVA, smeared, and stained with trichrome or iron hematoxylin, the gold-standard methods for intestinal protozoa. SAF (sodium acetate-formalin) is a single alternative fixative that supports concentration and, after processing, permanent staining. Many laboratories use a single vial system (for example, X-PVA or total-fix systems) to avoid splitting specimens. Whatever the vial, the rule that examiners repeat is this: formalin for concentration and wet mounts, PVA (or SAF) for the permanent stain - and if the laboratory receives only formalin, report that permanent staining is not possible rather than forcing a bad smear.

sections.heading: Wet mounts, concentration, and the stained smear
sections.body: The direct wet mount is the fastest screen: a small saline suspension examined under low power to find anything that moves or refracts, then high power to count and characterize. Sensitivity is modest - a well-known practical estimate is that a direct smear examines only a tiny fraction of the stool - so the formalin-ethyl acetate sedimentation concentration step is the workhorse of routine ova and parasite examinations. In this method the stool is strained through wet gauze to remove large debris, concentrated sediment is mixed with 10 percent formalin, ethyl acetate is added, centrifugation forms a plug of debris at the interface while parasites sediment, the debris plug is discarded, and the sediment is resuspended for wet mounts (saline and iodine). Concentration increases sensitivity for eggs, cysts, and larvae and is used on every routine stool in most protocols; it does not replace the permanent stain for identifying amebae. Permanent stained smears use PVA-fixed material spread thinly, allowed to dry, and stained with Wheatley trichrome (nuclear chromatin and chromatoid bars stand out in red-purple against green-blue cytoplasm) or iron hematoxylin (sharper nuclear detail, more laborious). These are the reference methods for intestinal protozoa and the only way to make a confident species call on small amebae. The modified acid-fast stain (cold Kinyoun or modified Ziehl-Neelsen) targets the coccidia: Cryptosporidium oocysts (4-6 micrometers) stain variably - some bright red, some pink ghosts - Cyclospora cayetanensis (8-10 micrometers) stains variably and autofluoresces under ultraviolet light, and Cystoisospora belli oocysts (20-33 micrometers) are the giants of the group. Auramine-rhodamine fluorescence is an efficient screening stain for coccidia, confirmed by acid-fast or immunofluorescent methods. Immunologic stool panels (EIA or DFA for Giardia, Cryptosporidium, E. histolytica antigen) are common and must be correlated with microscopy because antigen and morphology answer slightly different questions.

sections.heading: Amebae: the E. histolytica complex and the nuclear count trap
sections.body: The genus Entamoeba keeps two exam questions in permanent rotation. The first is the species problem: Entamoeba histolytica (tissue-invasive, causes amebic dysentery and liver abscess) and Entamoeba dispar (morphologically identical, non-pathogenic commensal) cannot be told apart by microscopy - not by cyst size, not by nuclear detail, not by chromatoid bars. Some laboratories also consider Entamoeba moshkovskii, which is likewise morphologically identical and increasingly recognized. The honest report from a stained smear is therefore 'E. histolytica/dispar complex'; a specific call requires an E. histolytica-specific antigen detection test or PCR. Cysts of the complex are 12-15 micrometers with up to four nuclei in the mature cyst, finely distributed peripheral chromatin, and chromatoid bars with smoothly rounded ends. The one morphologic feature that is specific for pathogenic E. histolytica is a trophozoite that has ingested red blood cells - erythrophagocytosis is considered diagnostic of invasive disease in the right clinical setting. The second question is the E. coli versus E. histolytica cyst comparison, and the discriminating features are nuclear number and texture: Entamoeba coli cysts are larger (15-25 micrometers, occasionally up to 50), mature cysts have up to eight nuclei, the peripheral chromatin is coarse and unevenly clumped, the karyosome is large and eccentric, immature cysts show a large glycogen mass (visible as a dark block with iodine), and chromatoid bars are blunt with splintered, ragged ends. Trophozoites follow the same logic: E. histolytica trophs move with directional, progressive motility and eat red cells; E. coli trophs are sluggish and ingest bacteria and debris. Related amebae round out the differential: Endolimax nana (tiny, 5-10 micrometer cysts, four nuclei with large karyosomes and no peripheral chromatin), Iodamoeba butschlii (one large nucleus, enormous glycogen vacuole, best seen with iodine), and Dientamoeba fragilis - which deserves its own note because it has no cyst stage at all, only fragile trophozoites (usually with two nuclei whose chromatin is fragmented into peripheral granules) and is transmitted in Enterobius eggs. A stool sent only for ova and parasites with no permanent stain will underreport the small amebae and Dientamoeba entirely.

sections.heading: Giardia, Cryptosporidium, and the coccidia
sections.body: Giardia lamblia (also called G. duodenalis or G. intestinalis) is the flagellate with the most recognizable silhouette in parasitology. The trophozoite is pear-shaped or teardrop-shaped, 10-20 micrometers long, with two nuclei, paired axostyles, and a ventral adhesive disc - the paired nuclei give the classic 'owl face' or 'flying bird' appearance in stained smears. Trophozoites are found in diarrheic stools and in duodenal aspirates or the string test (Entero-Test), because Giardia colonizes the duodenum and upper jejunum. The cyst is oval (8-12 micrometers), with 2-4 nuclei and curved median bodies that old textbooks describe as resembling 'old-fashioned spectacles' or a mustache; cysts are the stage passed in formed stools and the infective stage. Diagnosis uses concentration wet mounts, permanent stains, or - very commonly - Giardia stool antigen tests (EIA, immunochromatographic, or DFA), which are more sensitive than a single microscopic exam. Clinically Giardia causes bloating, foul-smelling fatty diarrhea, and malabsorption; outbreaks follow contaminated water, a favorite scenario setting. The coccidia head the opportunistic list. Cryptosporidium spp. oocysts are tiny (4-6 micrometers), round, modified acid-fast positive (with the characteristic mix of darkly stained and pale 'ghost' oocysts), and are detected more efficiently with immunofluorescent antibody or antigen EIA; transmission is waterborne (oocysts resist chlorination) and infection causes self-limited watery diarrhea in immunocompetent hosts but relentless, life-threatening secretory diarrhea in advanced HIV/AIDS. Cyclospora cayetanensis (8-10 micrometers) causes prolonged watery diarrhea, is variably acid-fast, and autofluoresces under ultraviolet microscopy; Cystoisospora (Isospora) belli oocysts are large (20-33 micrometers), ellipsoidal, acid-fast, and contain two sporocysts - when an exam gives you a giant acid-fast oocyst in a stool, the answer is Cystoisospora. All three respond to review questions asking which stool modification (modified acid-fast or fluorescence) is needed, because routine trichrome can miss the small coccidia entirely.

sections.heading: Helminth eggs and larvae: the stool lineup
sections.body: Helminth identification on stool is egg identification, with one famous exception. Ascaris lumbricoides produces the largest common eggs: fertilized eggs are 45-75 by 35-50 micrometers, round to oval, golden-brown, with a thick shell and a bumpy mammillated albuminoid coat (decorticated eggs lose the bumps and look smooth); unfertilized eggs are longer (85-95 micrometers), narrower, thin-shelled, and filled with disorganized refractile granules. Hookworm eggs (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus are indistinguishable by egg) are 55-75 by 36-40 micrometers, oval, thin-shelled, with a clear space between shell and a 4-8 cell morula - the classic 'segmented egg' of tropical stool exams. Trichuris trichiura eggs are unmistakable once seen: barrel- or lemon-shaped, 50-55 by 22-24 micrometers, bile-stained brown, with a smooth thick shell and clear mucoid plugs at both poles. Enterobius vermicularis eggs are D-shaped (one flattened side), 50-60 by 20-30 micrometers, and already contain a larva when passed - but they are deposited on the perianal skin, so routine stool examination is insensitive and the morning cellophane tape (Scotch tape) swab before bathing or defecation is the diagnostic procedure. Taenia eggs (T. solium and T. saginata) are 30-40 micrometers, spherical, with a thick radially striated embryophore surrounding an oncosphere with six hooklets; species differentiation needs the gravid proglottid (uterine branches: about 7-13 for T. solium, 13-35 for T. saginata) or the scolex (armed with hooks for T. solium, unarmed for T. saginata). This matters because T. solium eggs are infective to humans and cause cysticercosis - a favorite exam twist. Hymenolepis nana eggs have polar filaments between the embryophore and outer shell and are diagnostic of active infection because the egg can develop within the same host. Strongyloides stercoralis is the exception: stool usually contains larvae, not eggs - rhabditiform L1 larvae with a long buccal cavity and small genital primordium (hookworm L1 has a short buccal cavity and large genital primordium) and, in hyperinfection, filariform L3 larvae with notched tails. Agar plate culture and serology (EIA) improve Strongyloides detection, and screening matters before immunosuppression because autoinfection can produce hyperinfection syndrome. Finally, the Philippine favorite that mimics Trichuris: Capillaria philippinensis eggs (36-45 micrometers) are barrel-shaped like Trichuris but smaller, with flattened rather than rounded bipolar plugs, and cause malabsorption with autoinfection - when a stool exam in the Philippines shows 'small Trichuris,' think Capillaria.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: Entamoeba histolytica causes amebic colitis (bloody, mucoid diarrhea) and liver abscess; treating E. dispar is unnecessary, so accurate reporting prevents overtreatment - and missing E. histolytica delays care for invasive disease. Giardia is a leading cause of parasitic diarrhea worldwide and produces chronic malabsorption and failure to thrive in children. Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and Cystoisospora matter most in immunocompromised patients, where Cryptosporidium in advanced HIV/AIDS can be fatal without immune reconstitution. Ascaris burden causes obstruction and malnutrition in children; hookworm causes iron-deficiency anemia through chronic blood loss; Trichuris heavy infection causes dysentery and rectal prolapse; Strongyloides hyperinfection in immunosuppressed hosts carries high mortality and must be ruled out before steroids or transplant; Taenia solium eggs cause neurocysticercosis, a leading cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic areas including the Philippines. Correct stool diagnosis drives the right drug, the right duration, and the right public health action.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Report the examination actually performed: 'ova and parasite examination, concentration and permanent stained smear' plus the fixative received. Never report E. histolytica from morphology alone - use 'E. histolytica/dispar complex' unless an antigen or PCR test resolves the species. Flag specimens lacking a permanent stain (formalin only) as limited examinations, because small amebae and Dientamoeba will be underdetected. For Enterobius, document tape test results explicitly (number of tapes, time of collection); for Strongyloides, consider multiple stools, agar plate culture, and serology. Quantitate heavy infections when possible ('many Ascaris eggs per coverslip') because burden guides therapy and complication risk. Verify suspected artifacts at higher magnification and in iodine preparations, and remember that Charcot-Leyden crystals (slender bipyramidal crystals from eosinophil breakdown) support tissue-invasive helminth or amebic disease but are not diagnostic alone. Reference intervals do not apply to qualitative parasitology; the report is the identification, its stage, and a comment on method limitations, verified against local laboratory procedures.

examTraps: Trichuris eggs have rounded bipolar mucoid plugs and a barrel shape; hookworm eggs are thin-shelled with a 4-8 cell morula and no plugs - never confuse the two, and when a 'small Trichuris' appears in a Philippine stool, remember Capillaria philippinensis with flattened plugs.

E. histolytica and E. dispar are morphologically identical; only antigen or PCR separates them. E. coli is separated from E. histolytica by mature cyst nuclei count (up to 8 versus up to 4), coarse versus fine peripheral chromatin, and splintered versus rounded chromatoid bars.

A formalin-preserved specimen cannot produce a permanent stained smear; trichrome requires PVA (or SAF) fixed material. Reporting a trichrome from a formalin vial is a procedural impossibility examiners love to test.
Enterobius eggs are not reliably found on routine stool examination - the answer is the morning cellophane tape test before bathing or defecation.
Strongyloides stercoralis shows larvae (rhabditiform L1, long buccal cavity, small genital primordium) in stool, not eggs; hookworm L1 has a short buccal cavity and large genital primordium.

Artifacts mimic parasites: pollen grains (thick wall, uniform size, radial striations), yeast (budding, no internal organelles), starch granules (Maltese cross under polarized light), and air bubbles. Charcot-Leyden crystals suggest eosinophilic inflammation but are not parasites.

memoryHooks.text: PVA for the permanent stain, formalin for concentration and wet mounts - 'PVA Preserves the smear for stain; Formalin is for Finding eggs.'
memoryHooks.funny: Meow the cat: 'Pag formalin lang ang dala mo, wag ka nang mag-trichrome - hindi yan instant noodles na tubig lang ang kailangan!'

memoryHooks.text: Trichuris = barrel with two polar plugs; hookworm = morula in a thin shell; Enterobius = D-shaped egg on tape, not in stool.
memoryHooks.funny: Trichuris 'may dalawang plug' like a barrel na may two caps; hookworm naman, may baby cells sa loob na parang binalot na tapioca. 'Wag silang pagkamaliin - magkaiba ang klase ng bilao!'
